Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 109, verse 1–5:

Surah "al-Kafirun" (The Disbelievers). It is Meccan according to the view of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Ikrimah, and Medinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, and to Qatadah and al-Dahhak. It has six verses. In al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Anas, it is related that it is equal to one third of the Qur'an. In the book (al-Radd li-Abi Bakr al-Anbari): Abdullah ibn Najiyah informed us, saying: Yusuf narrated to us, saying: al-Qa'nabi and Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, from Musa ibn Wardan, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [("Say: O you disbelievers") is equal to one quarter of the Qur'an.] It was also narrated as a statement of Anas (mawquf). The hafiz Abu Muhammad Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) led his Companions in the dawn prayer during a journey, and he recited "Say: O you disbelievers" and "Say: He is Allah, the One," and then said: [I have recited to you one third of the Qur'an and one quarter of it.] Jubayr ibn Mut'im narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [Would you like, O Jubayr, when you set out on a journey, to be among the best of your companions in appearance and the most provisioned?] I said: Yes. He said: ("Recite these five surahs from the beginning of "Say: O you disbelievers" [al-Kafirun: 1] to "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind" [al-Nas: 1], and begin your recitation with "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"). He said: By Allah, I was not a man of much wealth, and when I traveled I was the most shabby in appearance [bidh al-hay'ah: its worn-out state], and the least provisioned among them. But since I recited them, I became among the best of them in appearance and the most provisioned, until I returned from that journey.

Farwah ibn Nawfal al-Ashja'i said: A man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Advise me. He said: (Recite at your sleeping time "Say: O you disbelievers," for it is a declaration of freedom from polytheism). Abu Bakr al-Anbari and others related it. Ibn 'Abbas said: There is nothing in the Qur'an more grievous to Iblis than it, because it is a declaration of Tawhid and freedom from polytheism. Al-Asma'i said: It used to be said of "Say: O you disbelievers" and "Say: He is Allah, the One" that they are al-Muqashqashatan, meaning that they clear one from hypocrisy. Abu Ubaydah said: Just as al-Hana' (tar: al-qatran) cleanses the mange and heals it. Ibn al-Sikkit said: It is said of a sore and smallpox when they dry up and scale, and of mange in camels when the skin hardens: its skin has become scaly, its skin has peeled, and its skin has flaked off.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Say: O you disbelievers. I do not worship what you worship. Nor are you worshipers of what I worship. Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped. Nor are you worshipers of what I worship.﴾

﴿Nor are you worshipers of what I worship.﴾

Ibn Ishaq and others related from Ibn 'Abbas that the occasion of its revelation was that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and Umayyah ibn Khalaf met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: O Muhammad, come, let us worship what you worship, and you worship what we worship, and we and you share in all our affairs. If what you have brought is better than what is in our hands, we will have shared it with you and taken our portion of it; and if what is in our hands is better than what is in your hand, you will have shared our affair and taken your portion of it. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "Say: O you disbelievers." Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): If you would touch [istalama: to touch it with the forehead or with the hand] some of these deities, we would believe you. So Jibril came down to the Prophet (ﷺ) with this surah, and they despaired of him, and harmed him and his Companions.

The "al" (the definite article) refers to the sense of the known, although it may be for the genus, insofar as it is an attribute of "ayy," because it addresses those who, in Allah's knowledge, are destined to die in their disbelief. So it is from the specific that came in the form of the general. Similar to this from al-Mawardi: It was revealed as a reply, and by "the disbelievers" he meant specific people, not all disbelievers, because among them are those who believed and worshiped Allah, and among them are those who died or were killed in their disbelief; and they are the ones addressed by this statement, and they are the ones mentioned.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever criticized the Qur'an recited: "Say to those who disbelieve: I do not worship what you worship," and claimed that this is the correct reading. That is a fabrication against the Lord of the worlds, a weakening of the meaning of this surah, and an annulment of what Allah intended, that His Prophet should humble the polytheists by addressing them with this stern address and obligating them to what every person of intellect and understanding finds repugnant. This is because the false wording he claims is included in the meaning of our recitation, and adds an interpretation not found in their falsehood and distortion. The meaning of our recitation is: "Say to those who disbelieve: O disbelievers." The evidence for the soundness of this is that when an Arab says to his addressee, "Say to Zayd, come to us," the meaning is "Say to Zayd: O Zayd, come to us." Thus our recitation covers everything they have, and the best wording and most eloquent meaning is preserved from their falsehood, since the Messenger, peace be upon him, would address them in their assembly, saying to them: "O you disbelievers." He knew that they would be angered at being attributed to disbelief and placed among its people, yet he was protected and safeguarded from any hand of theirs reaching him or any harm coming to him from them. Whoever does not recite "Say: O you disbelievers" as Allah revealed it has dropped a verse from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The way of the people of Islam is not to hasten to such a thing, nor to approach their Prophet by stripping him of the virtues that Allah granted him and honored him with.

As for the reason for the repetition, it has been said that it is for emphasis in cutting off their hopes, as you say: "By Allah, I will not do such-and-such," then "By Allah, I will not do it." Most scholars of meanings said: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and among their methods is repetition for the sake of emphasis and clarity, just as among their methods is brevity for the sake of lightness and conciseness, because the orator and speaker moving from one matter to another is better than limiting himself in the situation to a single matter. Allah the Exalted said: "So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?" [al-Rahman: 13]. "Woe, that Day, to the deniers" [al-Mutaffifin: 10]. "No! They will know. Then no! They will know" [al-Naba': 4-5]. "Indeed, with hardship is ease. Indeed, with hardship is ease" [al-Sharh: 5-6]. All of this is for emphasis.

A speaker may say: "Shoot, shoot! Hurry, hurry!" From it is his statement, peace be upon him, in the sound hadith: ("I will not permit, then I will not permit; Fatimah is a part of me"). Muslim related it. [The wording of the hadith as in Sahih Muslim (Book of Virtues): (... that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the pulpit saying: The sons of Hisham ibn al-Mughirah have asked my permission to marry their daughter to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, so I do not permit them. Then I do not permit them, then I do not permit them, unless Ibn Abi Talib wishes to divorce my daughter and marry their daughter; for my daughter is a part of me, what troubles her troubles me, and what harms her harms me.) "al-Bid'ah" (with fath, and sometimes with kasrah): a piece of flesh.]

The poet said:

"Why did you not ask the hosts of Kindah, on the day they turned back: where, where are we?"

Another said:

"O Bakr, bring Kulayb back to me! O Bakr, where, where is the flight?" [This verse is from the verses of al-Muhalhil ibn Rabi'ah, said after he avenged his brother Kulayb (see the tenth witness after the hundredth in Khizanat al-Adab).]

Another said:

"O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah! The best of all Tamim and the most noble of them!"

Another said:

"O al-Aqra' ibn Habis, O al-Aqra'! If your brother is struck down, you will be struck down!" [The verse is by Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, and it is said to be by 'Amr ibn Khatharim al-Bajali. (See Khizanat al-Adab, witness eighty-first after the five hundredth.)]

Another said:

"Ala ya aslami, thumma ya aslami, thumma aslami, wa thalath tahiyyat, wa in lam takallami."

And there are many similar examples. It has also been said: This is in accordance with their statement: "You worship our gods and we worship your God, then you worship our gods and we worship your God, then you worship our gods and we worship your God," so we go on in this manner forever, year after year. So they were answered to everything they said with its opposite, meaning that this will never happen. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): We will give you wealth to make you the richest man in Mecca, and marry you to whomever you wish, and we will follow your heels, meaning walk behind you, and you will stop insulting our gods. If you do not do so, then we offer you one thing, which is good for us and for you: you worship our gods al-Lat and al-'Uzza for a year, and we will worship your God for a year. [In the margin of al-Jamal, quoting al-Qurtubi: "Then you worship our gods, and we worship your God, and we continue in this forever: year and year. So it was revealed..." etc.] So the surah was revealed. Hence the repetition in "I do not worship what you worship" is because the people repeated their speech to him again and again. And Allah knows best. It has also been said: The repetition is for the sake of intensifying the rejection. It has also been said: That is, "I do not worship, in the present, what you worship, nor are you worshipers, in the present, of what I worship," and "I am not a worshiper, in the future, of what you have worshiped, nor are you in the future worshipers of what I worship." This was said by al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad. It has also been said: They used to worship idols; when they grew tired of one idol and wearied of worshiping it, they abandoned it, then took another idol by the desire of their souls. When they passed by stones that pleased them, they cast aside these and raised those, glorified them and set them up as gods to worship. So he, peace be upon him, was commanded to say to them: "I do not worship what you worship today of these gods that are before you." Then he said: "Nor are you worshipers of what I worship," since you worship only the idol you have taken, which is with you now. "Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped," meaning of yesterday's gods that you abandoned, turning instead to these. "Nor are you worshipers of what I worship."

So I worship my God. It has also been said: The Exalted's statement "I do not worship what you worship" and "Nor are you worshipers of what I worship" refer to the future. His statement "Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped" refers to the negation of worship from him regarding what they worshiped in the past. Then he said: "Nor are you worshipers of what I worship," repeated in wording but not in meaning, because the contrast would require: "Nor are you worshipers of what I have worshiped," but he deviated from the wording "I have worshiped" to "I worship," indicating that what was worshiped in the past is what is worshiped in the future, although the past and future may each occupy the place of the other. This occurs most often in Allah's reports. He said "what I worship" and did not say "whom I worship," to contrast with "Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped," since they are idols and images, and only "what" is appropriate for them, not "whom." So he took the first to match the second, so that the speech would correspond and not conflict. "What" has also been used for those who have intellect, as in their saying: "Glory to Him who subjected these to us." It has also been said: The meaning and its implication of the verses: "Say: O you disbelievers, I do not worship the idols you worship, nor are you worshipers of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whom I worship, because of your association with Him and your taking of idols. If you claim that you worship Him, then you are liars, because you worship Him as polytheists. So I do not worship what you worship, meaning like your worship. Here 'what' is a verbal noun (masdariyyah). Likewise, 'Nor are you worshipers of what I worship' is also masdariyyah, meaning: nor are you worshipers in the manner of my worship, which is monotheism."

The meaning of our recitation is: "Say to those who disbelieve: O disbelievers." The evidence for the soundness of this is that when an Arab says to his addressee, "Say to Zayd, come to us," the meaning is "Say to Zayd: O Zayd, come to us." Thus our recitation covers everything they have, and the best wording and most eloquent meaning is preserved from their falsehood, since the Messenger, peace be upon him, would address them in their assembly, saying to them: "O you disbelievers." He knew that they would be angered at being attributed to disbelief and placed among its people, yet he was protected and safeguarded from any hand of theirs reaching him or any harm coming to him from them. Whoever does not recite "Say: O you disbelievers" as Allah revealed it has dropped a verse from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The way of the people of Islam is not to hasten to such a thing, nor to approach their Prophet by stripping him of the virtues that Allah granted him and honored him with.

As for the reason for the repetition, it has been said that it is for emphasis in cutting off their hopes, as you say: "By Allah, I will not do such-and-such," then "By Allah, I will not do it." Most scholars of meanings said: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and among their methods is repetition for the sake of emphasis and clarity, just as among their methods is brevity for the sake of lightness and conciseness, because the orator and speaker moving from one matter to another is better than limiting himself in the situation to a single matter. Allah the Exalted said: "So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?" [al-Rahman: 13]. "Woe, that Day, to the deniers" [al-Mutaffifin: 10]. "No! They will know. Then no! They will know" [al-Naba': 4-5]. "Indeed, with hardship is ease. Indeed, with hardship is ease" [al-Sharh: 5-6]. All of this is for emphasis.

A speaker may say: "Shoot, shoot! Hurry, hurry!" From it is his statement, peace be upon him, in the sound hadith: ("I will not permit, then I will not permit; Fatimah is a part of me"). Muslim related it. [The wording of the hadith as in Sahih Muslim (Book of Virtues): (... that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the pulpit saying: The sons of Hisham ibn al-Mughirah have asked my permission to marry their daughter to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, so I do not permit them. Then I do not permit them, then I do not permit them, unless Ibn Abi Talib wishes to divorce my daughter and marry their daughter; for my daughter is a part of me, what troubles her troubles me, and what harms her harms me.) "al-Bid'ah" (with fath, and sometimes with kasrah): a piece of flesh.]

The poet said:

"Why did you not ask the hosts of Kindah, on the day they turned back: where, where are we?"

Another said:

"O Bakr, bring Kulayb back to me! O Bakr, where, where is the flight?" [This verse is from the verses of al-Muhalhil ibn Rabi'ah, said after he avenged his brother Kulayb (see the tenth witness after the hundredth in Khizanat al-Adab).]

Another said:

"O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah! The best of all Tamim and the most noble of them!"

Another said:

"O al-Aqra' ibn Habis, O al-Aqra'! If your brother is struck down, you will be struck down!" [The verse is by Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, and it is said to be by 'Amr ibn Khatharim al-Bajali. (See Khizanat al-Adab, witness eighty-first after the five hundredth.)]

Another said:

"Ala ya aslami, thumma ya aslami, thumma aslami, wa thalath tahiyyat, wa in lam takallami."

And there are many similar examples. It has also been said: This is in accordance with their statement: "You worship our gods and we worship your God, then you worship our gods and we worship your God, then you worship our gods and we worship your God," so we go on in this manner forever, year after year. So they were answered to everything they said with its opposite, meaning that this will never happen. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): We will give you wealth to make you the richest man in Mecca, and marry you to whomever you wish, and we will follow your heels, meaning walk behind you, and you will stop insulting our gods. If you do not do so, then we offer you one thing, which is good for us and for you: you worship our gods al-Lat and al-'Uzza for a year, and we will worship your God for a year. [In the margin of al-Jamal, quoting al-Qurtubi: "Then you worship our gods, and we worship your God, and we continue in this forever: year and year. So it was revealed..." etc.] So the surah was revealed. Hence the repetition in "I do not worship what you worship" is because the people repeated their speech to him again and again. And Allah knows best. It has also been said: The repetition is for the sake of intensifying the rejection. It has also been said: That is, "I do not worship, in the present, what you worship, nor are you worshipers, in the present, of what I worship," and "I am not a worshiper, in the future, of what you have worshiped, nor are you in the future worshipers of what I worship." This was said by al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad. It has also been said: They used to worship idols; when they grew tired of one idol and wearied of worshiping it, they abandoned it, then took another idol by the desire of their souls. When they passed by stones that pleased them, they cast aside these and raised those, glorified them and set them up as gods to worship. So he, peace be upon him, was commanded to say to them: "I do not worship what you worship today of these gods that are before you." Then he said: "Nor are you worshipers of what I worship," since you worship only the idol you have taken, which is with you now. "Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped," meaning of yesterday's gods that you abandoned, turning instead to these. "Nor are you worshipers of what I worship."

So I worship my God. It has also been said: The Exalted's statement "I do not worship what you worship" and "Nor are you worshipers of what I worship" refer to the future. His statement "Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped" refers to the negation of worship from him regarding what they worshiped in the past. Then he said: "Nor are you worshipers of what I worship," repeated in wording but not in meaning, because the contrast would require: "Nor are you worshipers of what I have worshiped," but he deviated from the wording "I have worshiped" to "I worship," indicating that what was worshiped in the past is what is worshiped in the future, although the past and future may each occupy the place of the other. This occurs most often in Allah's reports. He said "what I worship" and did not say "whom I worship," to contrast with "Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped," since they are idols and images, and only "what" is appropriate for them, not "whom." So he took the first to match the second, so that the speech would correspond and not conflict. "What" has also been used for those who have intellect, as in their saying: "Glory to Him who subjected these to us." It has also been said: The meaning and its implication of the verses: "Say: O you disbelievers, I do not worship the idols you worship, nor are you worshipers of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whom I worship, because of your association with Him and your taking of idols. If you claim that you worship Him, then you are liars, because you worship Him as polytheists. So I do not worship what you worship, meaning like your worship. Here 'what' is a verbal noun (masdariyyah). Likewise, 'Nor are you worshipers of what I worship' is also masdariyyah, meaning: nor are you worshipers in the manner of my worship, which is monotheism."

It contains the sense of a threat, like His saying ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾ [al-Qasas: 55] [[Verse 55 of Surah al-Qasas.]]. That is, "If you are content with your religion, then we are content with ours." This was before the command to fight, and it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword. It was also said that the whole surah is abrogated, and it was also said that nothing in it was abrogated, because it is a statement of fact.

The meaning of ﴿For you is your religion﴾ is: the recompense of your religion is for you, and the recompense of my religion is for me. He called their religion "religion" because they believed in it and adhered to it. It was also said that the meaning is: your recompense is for you and my recompense is for me, because religion (dīn) means recompense.

Nafi', al-Bazzi (on the authority of Ibn Kathir, with a variant reported from him), Hisham (on the authority of Ibn Amir), and Hafs (on the authority of Asim) read the yā' in ﴿wa-liya dīn﴾ with a fatha. Ibn Asim, Salam and Ya'qub kept the yā' in ﴿dīnī﴾ in both pause and continuation. They said: "Because it is a noun, like the kāf in ﴿dīnikum﴾ and the tā' in ﴿qumtu﴾." The rest read it without a yā', like His saying ﴿Then He will guide me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78] and ﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50], and similar, relying on the kasra and following the orthography of the mushaf (the written codex of the Qur'an), since it was written in it without a yā'.
